title: Environment Variables & Configuration
summary: Environment variables let a Next.js app read settings from its runtime environment.

subtopics.title: Local settings
subtopics.explanation: Environment files let a developer store settings such as a local API address. The app reads the values instead of scattering them through code. This is like changing a route on a map without redrawing every road. Keep a sample file with placeholder values so teammates know what names they need. For example, use a local base URL for development and a production URL in host settings.

subtopics.title: Server-only values
subtopics.explanation: Server-only variables are read by code that runs on the server. They can hold private credentials if the server never returns them to the browser. Think of them as keys kept by the building manager. Check the code path carefully: sending a value in a page response makes it public even if it began as a server variable. For example, a public analytics ID can be exposed only if the service defines it as public.

subtopics.title: Public prefix
subtopics.explanation: Next.js exposes variables prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` to browser code. Anyone can inspect the built JavaScript and see those values. The prefix is like putting a notice on a public bulletin board. Use it only for information safe for every visitor, such as a public analytics identifier, never passwords or private tokens. For example, never prefix a database password with NEXT_PUBLIC_.

subtopics.title: Secrets
subtopics.explanation: Never commit real secrets to Git. A repository may be copied, logged, or shared, and deleting a secret later does not erase every copy. Treat a leaked key like a lost house key: replace it, revoke the old one, and review access. Store production values in the hosting provider’s protected configuration. For example, keep a sample env file with names and safe placeholder values.

subtopics.title: Restart
subtopics.explanation: Next.js reads environment files during development or build startup. Restart the server after changing them so the new values are loaded. It is like restarting an appliance after changing its settings. For each environment, verify which values are available and fail clearly when a required setting is missing. For example, verify required settings in both preview and production builds.

foundations.overview: Environment variables are named settings supplied to an app while it runs or builds. In Next.js, the same setting can be available only on the server or deliberately included in browser code. Think of them like labeled drawers: public settings go in the shared room, while secrets stay in a locked office. Keep real credentials private, document required names, and never place secrets in source control.
foundations.whyItMatters: Environment settings let one codebase work in local, preview, and production contexts. Correct boundaries prevent leaked credentials and configuration mismatches.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser only ever sees NEXT_PUBLIC_ values because Next literally replaces process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_X with the string at build time. Any non-prefixed variable simply doesn't exist in client JavaScript — referencing it there yields undefined.
foundations.realWorldUsage: NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL or a public analytics key go in the public bucket; DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, and auth secrets stay server-only and are read in route handlers/server components.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct handling prevents costly secret leaks and outages, and lets one build run across environments by changing server-side variables — speeding delivery and reducing risk.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Clear public/private separation and startup validation reduce a whole class of bugs (undefined config, leaked keys) and make onboarding easier via a documented .env.example.
foundations.performanceImpact: Inlining NEXT_PUBLIC_ values at build time means zero runtime cost to read them, but it also means they're frozen until the next build — a trade-off to plan for when a public value must change.
commonUseCases: Exposing a public API base URL or analytics key via NEXT_PUBLIC_
Keeping database URLs and secret keys server-only
Validating required env vars at startup with Zod for typed, safe access

commonMisconceptions.myth: Any environment variable is automatically private/secure.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only non-prefixed variables are server-only; NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined into the browser bundle and visible to everyone.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Changing a NEXT_PUBLIC_ value updates the app immediately.
commonMisconceptions.reality: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are baked in at BUILD time, so you must rebuild/redeploy for the change to take effect.

commonMisconceptions.myth: process.env values are guaranteed to exist and be typed.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They're string | undefined; without validation a missing or malformed variable silently breaks things at runtime.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An environment file keeps its values secret automatically.
commonMisconceptions.reality: If a value is bundled into client code or committed, users or collaborators can inspect it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Restarting a page refreshes every server setting.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The development server or build process usually must reload environment values.

config.intro: Follow how Next decides whether a variable stays server-only or ships to the client.

steps.name: Declare
steps.detail: You add a variable to a .env file, e.g. DATABASE_URL=... or NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=...

steps.name: Load
steps.detail: At startup/build, Next loads .env files into process.env, applying precedence (.env.local overrides .env).

steps.name: Check prefix
steps.detail: Next checks the name: does it start with NEXT_PUBLIC_? That single rule decides client visibility.

steps.name: Inline (public)
steps.detail: If prefixed, the value is statically inlined into the client bundle at build time — visible in the browser, frozen until rebuild.

steps.name: Keep private (server)
steps.detail: If NOT prefixed, the value stays in server process.env only; client bundles never receive it.

steps.name: Use safely
steps.detail: Read public values anywhere; read secrets only in server code, ideally through a validated, typed env object.

codeLab.title: Sort variables into public vs server-only
codeLab.instructions: Given four variables, decide which need the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix (safe for the browser) and which must stay server-only. Edit the component to fill in each verdict, then Run. (Analytics site ID; database password; public API base URL; auth signing secret.)
codeLab.expectedOutput: Each variable labeled public (NEXT_PUBLIC_) or server-only.
hints: If the browser needs to read it, it must be NEXT_PUBLIC_ — and therefore is NOT secret.
Anything sensitive (passwords, signing keys, DB URLs) must stay server-only with no prefix.

keyTakeaways: Environment files let a developer store settings such as a local API address.
Server-only variables are read by code that runs on the server.
Never commit real secrets to Git.
